title: [A-Za-z ]+ rejects "Anne-Marie", "O'Brien", and anyone with an accent in their name
assumption: A simple letters-and-spaces regex is a reasonable baseline check for 'is this a real name'.

input.description: A 'name must contain only letters' validator on a signup or checkout form, written against the ASCII alphabet.

what_goes_wrong: Entirely ordinary names are rejected outright: an accented letter, a hyphen joining two given names, or an apostrophe in a surname all fail a check that was only ever tested against plain ASCII names.
why: The character class [A-Za-z] matches only the 26 unaccented Latin letters in each case; it has no entries for accented Latin letters, hyphens, apostrophes, or any non-Latin script at all. Any name that uses punctuation that is a normal part of that name, or any letter outside the ASCII range, fails the match even though the input is a perfectly ordinary name.
affects: any regex validator built on [A-Za-z] or similar ascii-only classes

repros.code:
import re
pattern = re.compile(r"^[A-Za-z ]+$")
for name in ["Zo\u00eb Navarro-Pe\u00f1a", "Anne-Marie", "O'Brien", "Jose Luis"]:
    print(name, bool(pattern.match(name)))
repros.expected_output:
Zoë Navarro-Peña False
Anne-Marie False
O'Brien False
Jose Luis True

Zoë Navarro-Peña false
Anne-Marie false
O'Brien false
Jose Luis true

fix: Don't validate names against a character allowlist at all if you can avoid it; if you must reject something, reject on length or control characters, not on script or punctuation — a name field should accept Unicode letters, marks, hyphens, and apostrophes at minimum.

sources.title: Patrick McKenzie: Falsehoods Programmers Believe About Names

test_cases.note: Your name validator should accept this; if it's built on an ASCII letter class, it won't.
